analysis.one_liner: Requires proof before your phone company can be switched and bans unauthorized charges on phone bills.
analysis.headline: The consumer anti-fraud bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 1999 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted two common phone-industry scams: "slamming," where a company switches your long-distance or local carrier without your permission, and "cramming," where third parties slip unauthorized charges onto your phone bill. It would have required companies to verify — with the customer affirmatively confirming — any request to change service, made customers not liable for unauthorized switches, imposed fines of $40,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for repeat violations, added criminal penalties of up to a year in prison, and barred phone companies from cutting off service over disputed third-party charges. It also gave the Federal Trade Commission power over deceptive practices by telecom carriers and required quarterly complaint reports so regulators could spot repeat offenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Telephone subscribers, especially people who don't closely review their phone bills. Every household with a phone line was exposed to slamming and cramming, which charged consumers for services they never ordered and could silently switch their carrier. The bill would have given them verification of any carrier change, written notice within 15 days, a toll-free number to dispute charges, and immunity from paying for fraudulent charges.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a subscriber to affirmatively confirm any switch of local or long-distance carrier, and makes the subscriber not liable for service changed without authorization [S3].

Bars anyone from putting a charge on a phone bill unless the customer specifically and knowingly authorized it, and requires bills to identify each company's charges and a toll-free dispute number [S2][S3].
Prohibits a phone company from disconnecting service over a disputed third-party charge, so consumers can fight a bogus fee without losing their phone line [S3].

Imposes fines of at least $40,000 for a first unauthorized switch and $100,000 for each later one, plus criminal penalties of up to one year in prison (five for repeat offenders), and lets the FCC bar convicted companies from operating [S3].

Gives the FTC authority over unfair or deceptive practices by telecom carriers and requires the FCC to feed complaint data to the FTC's Consumer Sentinel fraud database monthly, so repeat offenders can be identified [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telecommunications carriers and resellers that profited from unauthorized switches would face fines, criminal exposure, and possible disqualification. Third-party companies and billing agents that placed charges on phone bills — from voicemail and entertainment services to outright scams — would lose the ability to bill first and answer questions later, and would bear new disclosure, toll-free dispute line, and reporting costs. Local phone companies, which handled billing for third parties, would carry quarterly complaint-reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Telecom carriers and third-party billing companies

drawbacks.text: Requiring five affirmative confirmations and retained verification records adds compliance costs and friction, which carriers argued would slow legitimate switching and competitive entry into local and long-distance markets [S3].
Giving the FTC overlapping jurisdiction with the FCC over telecom carriers creates dual enforcement and potential confusion about which agency's rules apply [S3].
Local exchange carriers bear quarterly reporting obligations and, since they took a cut of third-party charges billed through phone bills, would lose some billing revenue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer side is strong: verification, notice, and disconnection protection directly target frauds that took real money from ordinary households. The main costs are compliance friction on carriers and some duplication between the FCC and FTC. On balance the bill was a conventional, well-structured consumer protection measure; its worst flaw was that Congress never examined it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on day one and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Susan Collins introduced the Telephone Services Fraud Prevention and Enforcement Act on January 19, 1999, joined by Senators Durbin and Jeffords [S1][S3][S5].
It attracted five cosponsors — four Democrats and one Republican — showing bipartisan interest [S4].

The entire action history after introduction is a single entry: the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telecom resellers and third-party billing companies that made money from unauthorized carrier switches and unapproved charges on phone bills were better off with the bill dead, since the fines, criminal penalties, and disqualification provisions never took effect. Local phone companies avoided new complaint-reporting and billing-disclosure duties.

for.name: Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push to curb slamming and cramming

for.name: 4 Senate Democrats and 1 Senate Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total bipartisan support to six senators including the sponsor

against.name: John McCain
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or scheduled it for consideration during the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor with four Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — and there is no record of any organized opposition, because the bill never reached a hearing or a vote.

industries.industry: Telecom resellers and long-distance carriers that used unauthorized switching
industries.note: Slammers switched customers' carriers without consent to capture their long-distance revenue. The bill's verification, fine, criminal, and disqualification provisions were aimed squarely at this business model.

industries.industry: Third-party service providers and billing agents (crammers)
industries.note: These companies placed voicemail, entertainment, and other charges on phone bills, sometimes unauthorized. The bill would ban unapproved charges, require itemized disclosure and toll-free dispute lines, and extend FCC penalties to non-carrier billing entities.

They would take on quarterly complaint-reporting duties and lose the per-charge cut they collected for billing third-party services, but the ban on disconnecting service over disputed third-party charges also reduced their collections leverage.
